Welcome to 45/15 sessions.

Summary
*   THE BASIC PRINCIPLE. Double threshold is really one long session with a long break in the middle. You concentrate load into a receptive window, then recover fully before the next block. Total quality volume rises while the number of days with elevated muscle tone falls.
*   WHAT THE RESEARCH SHOWS. The NTNU study found that splitting 6 × 10 minutes into two sessions of 3 × 10 minutes produced lower heart rate, lower lactate, and less muscle soreness the next day— despite identical total volume. The body responds more favorably to the split.
*   NOT JUST FOR ELITES. A 45-minute 10K runner can split 40 minutes of threshold work into a morning and evening session, stay fresher, and over a month double total threshold volume. Weekend placement works well for those with demanding weekdays.
*   THE BIGGEST PITFALL. The morning session run too hard. It should start 5-10 seconds per kilometer slower than target pace. Morning intervals are always slower than evening intervalsexpect a gap of 10-15 seconds per kilometer between 6-minute morning intervals and 1-minute evening intervals.
*   GRADUAL ENTRY. Start with two easy runs on the same day for 4-6 weeks. Then easy morning plus threshold evening. Then double threshold with pace well below actual threshold. Evaluate recovery before progressing.
*   FREQUENCY. Maximum one, occasionally two double days per week for experienced recreational runners. Double threshold is almost seductive when it works-resist the temptation to do it every day.
*   THREE LIMITATIONS OF PURE THRESHOLD WORK. Time efficiency for runners with limited hours, speed scagnation from training in a narrow pace range, and mental monotony over months and years. These limitations lead to the next chapter: 45/15 sessions.

Billat and Bangsbo
Véronique Billat won the Sierre-Zinal mountain race in 1982, the same race Kilian Jornet has won ten times. Not long after her competitive peak, she turned to physiology to better understand fatigue, adaptation, and individualized training
That decision launched an academic career spanning more than 200 scientific publications, and a simple question drove much of her research: how can runners spend the most time possible at maximum oxygen uptake?
I read her work with intense interest. She had published groundbreaking research on interval training at vO,max, the lowest speed that elicits maximum oxygen uptake. This meant short repetitions where pace sat at or around this intensity. After years of research, she had discovered how to maximize time at VO, max, and she adapted traditional 3-minute intervals into what is now known as Billat 30/30 intervals: 30 seconds of effort followed by 30 seconds of recovery.
Here was a researcher asking the same questions I had been grappling with since I was 14 years old and did my first lactate test. How do you get maximum effect in minimum time? How do you outsmart the body's regulatory systems?
Billar's breakthrough came when she discovered that by alternating between 30 seconds at 100% of VO_max and 30 seconds at 50% of that intensity, runners could keep oxygen uptake near VO_max far longer than during hard, continuous efforts at nearly the same intensity, typically several minutes near VO_max during the session (Billat et al., 2000).
In the study, they compared the 30/30 protocol against continuous running at around 91% of vO,max pace and found that 30/30 produced significantly more time at VO_max (approximately 7:51 vs. 2:42 minutes, with an average of 19 intervals), although individual variation was substantial. The findings opened up entirely new ways of thinking about interval training.
Parallel to Billa's work, the Danish physiologist Jens Bangsbo had published research on soccer players. His 1994 doctoral thesis, "The Physiology of Soccer: With Special Reference to Intense Intermittent Exercise," showed how football players naturally performed repeated high-intensity runs followed by short recovery periods.
Bangsbo was particularly interested in what happened metabolically during these brief, intense work periods. He found that even though players performed low-intensity activities for over 70% of the match, heart rate and body temperature were consistent with an average oxygen uptake of around 70% of maximum, much higher than expected based on activity level alone.
This phenomenon interested me immediately. Could this "metabolic inertia" be exploited in structured training, and perhaps amplified further?
45/15 Intervals
These discoveries set my mind working and launched extensive experimentation to find the optimal session, one that could exploit the underlying principles even better while building on existing knowledge of threshold training. It took time and comprehensive testing before the conclusion landed on 45/15:
45 seconds of running effort followed by 15 seconds of rest.

With 30/30, the work period felt too short. The body did not have time to setle properly into the work zone. There were too many transitions, and it was dificult to maintain even intensity as measured by lactate. With 60/20, the work period became too long and lactate accumulation too high. Maintaining speed through the entire session proved difficult. Muscular load became excessive, and total work time dropped due to accumulated fatigue. But 45/15 turned out to be the sweet spot.
WHY 45/15 WORKS
*   Perfect balance between work and rest
*   Enough time to establish high aerobic activation
*   Short enough pause to prevent full recovery
*   Lactate held stable at the desired level
*   Surprisingly, almost shockingly, short muscular recovery time
Many runners also experience something else unexpected: they maintain higher average heart rate through the entire session, including the pauses, than during almost any other hard workout, yet the post-session fatigue feels far less severe.
Cellular Adaptations
A series of important adaptations occur during 45/15 sessions. This section gets somewhat technical, but the science is compelling enough to include.
THE SCIENCE BEHIND 45/15
Lactate oscillations. 45/15 creates controlled oscillations around the threshold level. Lactate rises during the 45 seconds of work and falls partially during the 15-second pause. With each repetition, lactate production increases, but not to the point of progressive accumulation.
The 15 seconds allow partial lactate clearance and rapid ATP replen-ishment-ATP being the muscle's immediate energy currency-so that the next repetition starts under control. The result is continuous work

near the threshold without progressive accumulation, and with stable energy availability.
Mitochondrial biogenesis. High-intensity interval training, including 45/15 sessions, stimulates what we call mitochondrial biogenesis and improves mitochondrial function in the muscles (Little et al., 2010). Mitochondria are small power plants in each muscle cell that convert nutrients into energy. The more you have, and the better they work, the better your endurance becomes.
Metabolic flexibility. The frequent alternation between effort and rest can actually produce better effects than continuous work or traditional intervals. Over time, the body builds more mitochondria and enzymes that allow you to use oxygen more efficiently and burn both fat and carbohydrates into ATP, the fuel for muscles. At the same time, you do not lose the ability to produce rapid energy when speed is high. 45/15 builds a strong endurance engine without losing punch at high speeds (Egan & Zierath, 2013). The result is what we call metabolic flexibility: the body's ability to quickly and efficiently switch between different energy sources depending on what the situation demands.
Practical Application
So what does all this science mean for you on the training field? What you get from a 45/15 session is an elegant balance between load and recovery. That is why I always recommend one to two such sessions per week for recreational runners who want the best possible effect in limited time. These sessions also work excellently as X-sessions, meaning sessions with intensity well above the threshold. The particular structure and timing of pauses relative to efforts makes them perfect for this type of work as well.
This means 45/15 sessions can be used both as pure threshold sessions and as high-intensity sessions above the threshold. The short intervals permit relatively high speeds without excessive load.
I have experienced personally that this training form makes it possible to maintain fitness while staying injury-free over time. This is not genetics or luck, but intelligent intensity management. And 45/15 sits at the center of that.

Volume Progression
	• Week 1-2: 15 repetitions
	• Week 3-4: 20 repetitions
	• Week 5-6: 25 repetitions
	• Week 7-8: 30 repetitions or 2 sets of 15 with 1-2 min rest between
Standard Protocol (At or Just Above Threshold)
*   5-10 min warm-up and cool-down
*   15-30 × (45 sec work / 15 sec rest)
*   Intensity: 80-95% of maximum heart rate
*   Speed: Typically starts at 10-15K pace, progresses toward 3-5K pace
*   On treadmill: Increase by 0.1-0.2 km/h (0.1 mph) per interval
PROGRESSION PRINCIPLES ALONG MULTIPLE AXES
Intensity Progression
*   Constant speed: All intervals at the same pace, either pure threshold sessions or above threshold pace
*   Linear progression: Increase by 0.2-0.3 km/h (0.1 mph) every 5th interval, or 0.1 km/h per interval
*   Staircase progression: Groups of 5 at increasing speeds
*   Pyramid progression: Up to maximum speed, then back down
Recovery variation:
*   Standard: 15 seconds standing or walking
*   Active: 15 seconds light jagging (easiest outdoors)
Progressive Combination Variant
A favorite for many is a combination variant that incorporates elements from all the models. You start with 15-20 progressive 45/15 intervals on the treadmill, increasing speed by 0.1 km/h for each interval. The goal is that you should just barely manage the final two or three intervals before hitting the wall com-pletely. But here comes the twist. After two minutes of rest, you continue with five more intervals. These are performed, and this is the key, at the same speed you held on the last interval before the pause. Experience shows you will just
barely manage them.
Chapter 8 45/15

The Combination Variant - Step by Step
Start with 15-20 × 45/15 intervals on treadmill
2. Increase speed by 0.1 km/h for each interval
3. Goal: You should just barely manage the final 2-3 intervals before hitting
the wall
4. Take 2 min rest
1.    Continue with 5 more intervals at the same speed as your last interval before the pause
2.    Experience shows you will just barely manage these 5 intervals as well
Why does this work so well? You combine progressive loading with an intensive finishing focus. The gradual increase in the first part builds lactate levels in a controlled manner, while the final five intervals require you to maintain quality when the legs have already been pushed hard. The pauses both contribute and limit simultaneously.
In terms of intensity, you hit exactly where you should be: challenging enough to produce adaptation, but not so hard that the session becomes excessively damaging.
Here you combine threshold training with above-threshold training in a single session. Recent research on cyclists supports this approach. A 10-week study on well-trained cyclists showed that short intervals (30/15) produce greater improvements in both VOmax and pertormance than effort-matched 4-5 minute intervals (Rønnestad et al., 2015).
In later studies with shorter training periods, multiple sessions with short repetitions also show clearly better improvement in pertormance indicators than more traditional long intervals, even though VO_max does not always change as much over just a few weeks. A single study from the same research group also demonstrates that 30-second repetitions produce more time above 90% of maximum oxygen uptake than longer repetitions (Rønnestad et al., 2020).
Alternative Protocols
Although I favor 45/15, Billat's original 30/30 protocol (or Rønnestad's 30/15) has its advantages. for runners with lower threshold where speed becomes limiting, or when returning after illness or training breaks, you might choose
30/30 over 45/15 early in the training period.

Pyramid Variant	
1.	3 × 30 sec
2.	3 × 45 sec
3.	3 × 60 sec
4.	3x45 sec
	5. 3 × 30 sec
	6. (All with 15 seconds rest)
This variation allows higher intensity on the shorter intervals while the longer intervals build somewhat higher load.
Block Sets
Set 1: 10x45/15 at your 10K pace, 3 min rest
1.    Set 2: 10 x 45/15 at your 5K pace, 3 min rest
2.    Set 3: 10 × 45/15 at your 3K pace
This permits higher total quality and specific adaptation to race demands. In the transition between winter and spring seasons, precisely this type of block set can be an effective way to adapt to higher loads.
Combination Runs After Long Runs An undervalued element is the combination run.
Toward the end of a marathon, muscular factors in addition to metabolic ones limit performance. By adding 10-15 repetitions of 45/15 immediately after a 1-2 hour run, without any break, you stimulate the body to handle this type of fatigue with relatively low cost.
You go straight into the first 45-second repetition without a water break or anything else. The 15-second pauses should in this case be active pauses with light jogging. This is an unusual variant, and I have not seen it described in running literature, but it is likely a simple path to an important adaptation, especially for marathon preparation.

Combination Run - Protocol
1.
1-2 hours of completely easy running under 70% of max heart rate
2. Without any pause, straight into the first 45-second interval at intensity right around your threshold
Light jogging pause of 15 seconds
3.
1.    Repeat 10-15 times, preferably slightly progressive (faster and faster with each 45 seconds)
2.    Easy cool-down
This is a session that should be followed by completely easy training the next day. Even though it may appear minimally demanding with only a few extra 45/15 repetitions after a normal long run, the combination is sufficiently specific and loading in itself that it should always be followed by a completely easy training day.
You can expect the legs to feel like jelly the first time you do this. But after two or three sessions, it will feel better and better. That is a classic sign of a highly specific adaptation that you will benefit from toward the end of longer races.
Periodization Through the Season
Periodization means that each training phase has a somewhat different structure and content. Here, 45/15 sessions can be used precisely to provide different loading depending on where you are in your training work and how far you are from your goal.
Base Training
In early season, 45/15 is used to build pure aerobic capacity with minimal stress:
Base training
*   1-2 times per week
*   15-20 repetitions
*   Moderate progression

Specific Preparation Period
Approaching the season, focus shifts to increased specificity and intensity:
Specific preparation
*   1 time per week
*   20-30 repetitions or multiple sets
*   Speed progression toward race pace
*   Combination with other quality sessions
*   Consider pyramid variants or vary with set breaks
*   If training for marathon, try combination runs as described above
Competition Period
During the competition period, 45/15 can be used for maintenance and light sharpening:
	Competition period
	• Every 10-14 days
	• 12-15 repetitions at high intensity
	• Not to exhaustion
Return After Illness
45/15 is also one of the most effective things you can do after periods ofillness or breaks. It gets you back to normal form remarkably quickly. Have you been down with the flu and lost training? Few things compare to the progression that 2-3 × 45/15 sessions per week will deliver over the following two weeks while you rebuild volume before returning to normal training. It is extremely effective and simultaneously carries low risk.
Both as an elite athlete and now as a recreational runner, 45/15 is my standard for quickly lifting myself back up after illness, after first becoming healthy enough, of course. You return rapidly to proper muscular status, fitness builds back extremely quickly, and injury risk remains low. Exactly what you need after a period of sickness.

Later in this book, I will go through so-called double threshold training. 4515 and double threshold complement each other perfectly. But as a small previer; 45/15 can be used for those who want to try the double threshold variant, What typically works best is running 45/15 in the evening, while the morning consists of longer intervals, for example on the way to work or controlled on
the treadmill.
Double threshold example
*   Morning: 5 × 6 minutes threshold
*   Evening: 20-25 × 45/15
This combination means longer running intervals from the morning into a 45/15 session that sits at the other end of the training spectrum, and you simultaneously break up the muscular pattern before the next training session.
Distance-Specific Adaptation
45/15 intervals can be adapted for different distances, even though the basic principle remains the same. This applies where 45/15 is used as an intensive session above the threshold. If you are not targeting any particular distance but simply want to stay in the best possible shape, a variation of all these can work well. The most intensive variants toward 800-1500 meters should nevertheless be used with caution, due to somewhat higher injury risk.
For 800 and 1500-meter runners: Higher intensity, up toward 90-95% of max heart rate, with shorter total volume of 12-15 repetitions. Set breaks of 2-3 minutes work well here, and you can experiment with longer variants such as 60/20 or 75/25. The focus lies on somewhat higher speed, preferably
divided into block sets as described earlier.
For DK and IOk runners; The standard 45/15 protocol often works well, pace through the session. This is typically performed once per week during the with 20-30 repetitions, preferably with progression from threshold to 3-5K buildup period and provides the perfect balance between volume and intensity
for these distances.
For half marathon and marathon runners: Longer variants such as 60/20 can be considered, but with lower relative intensity at 85-90% of max heart rate.
And as described above, consider adding combination runs with 1-2 hours of running first, before 10-15 × 45/15 to finish. If you have run a marathon, you will recognize the sensation this type of session readily provokes.
Practical Advice
We close this chapter with some summarizing guidance:
Summary
*   Start carefully, always. It is better to finish faster on the last intervals than to collapse halfway through.
*   Do not do 45/15 the day after hard sessions. This is a quality session that requires fresh legs.
*   Vary the surface. Regular variation in running surface reduces overuse injuries for many, but beginners often prefer the treadmill for best possible pace control.
*   After illness, adjust interval length. Consider 15 seconds work with 45 seconds rest, or 30/30.
*   In combination with strength training. 45/15 after strength training provides faster recovery in my experience, and you sneak in conditioning and strength together. If you do this, it is especially important to start carefully and do a progressive variant as described above.
*   Use 45/15 year-round, but adapt. Longer variants in base training, shorter and more intense approaching the competition phase.
An Effective, Universal Method
45/15 intervals build VO,max, lactate threshold, and muscular power simul-rancously. Few other session types do this as effectively in my experience. The unique combination of high intensity and frequent pauses creates a training load that is both potent and sustainable. Many find it almost mind-bending that they can maintain such high intensity for so long without dragging the load with them deep into the training week, That is what makes it such a Perfect integration with a comprehensive threshold-based training program.
When these principles are followed, 45/15 offers a path to significant performance improvements across all distances from 1500 meters to marathon.
The method is universal and equally fective for the recreational runner who wants to break 50 minutes for 10K as for the elite athlete. But what if you want to take it one step further?
A Method for Those Who Want to Explore Further The combination of easy long runs, systematic threshold sessions, and 45/15 intervals provides all the training stimulus needed for significant progress. For most runners, this is more than enough. With Part II, you have the sessions.
Threshold, 45/15, weekly structures. You know what to do and why.
But knowing what to do is not the same as making it work over time. Most runners have experienced periods where everything looks right on paper, yet the body does not respond as it should, or periods where progress suddenly stops, or minor injuries that force a break just when you had found your rhythm.

The causes are concrete and recognizable: volume increased too quickly, too little sleep, transitions in surface or shoes, accumulated stiffness that never gets time to release. Things that are manageable individually, but that together break continuity.
Part III is about avoiding exactly that, and we will learn more about it in the next section, which steers the balance in the method even further.

Summary
*  WHY 45/15. 30/30 was too short to settle into the work zone. 60/20 pushed lactate too high. 45/15 hit the sweet spot: enough time to establish high acrobic activation, short enough pause to prevent full recovery, and surprisingly fast muscular recovery afterward.
*   DUAL PURPOSE. 45/15 works both as a threshold session and as an above threshold X-session. The short interval structure permits relatively high speeds without excessive muscular load building VO, max, lactate threshold, and running economy simultaneously.
*   PROGRESSION ALONG MULTIPLE AXES. Volume (15 reps up to 30 over eight weeks), intensity (constant, linear, staircase, or pyramid, and pause type (stand-ing, walking, or active jog). The combination variantprogressive intervals to near-failure, two minutes rest, then five more at the final speedmerges threshold and above-threshold work in a single session.
*   COMBINATION RUNS. Adding 10-15 reps of 45/15 immediately after a 1-2 hour easy run, with no break, simulates late-race fatigue at low cost. Legs feel like jelly the first time. After two or three sessions, adaptation is rapid and directly transferable to racing.
*   RETURN AFTER ILLNESS. Two to three 45/15 sessions per week for two weeks while rebuilding volume is one of the fastest, lowest-risk ways to restore fitness and muscular status after a break.
• DISTANCE-SPECIFIC ADAPTATION. Higher intensity and shorter volume for 800-1500m runners. Standard 20-30 reps with progression for 5K-10K. Longer variants (60/20) at lower relative intensity for half-marathon and marathon, with combination runs as a key tool.

he challenge for most runners is not finding yet another session. It's getting the same sessions to work week after week, without the body gradually protesting. The Norwegian Method gives you unusually good control, but the method gets even stronger when you are equally precise about health and total load. That's how you sustain the method for years, with minimal interruptions.
I competed in the Olympics in 2004 and started medical school in Oslo the same month. I finished my degree in 2010. The medical lens here is not a detour from the method. It's a framework that keeps the method on track: what typically breaks continuity, how you catch it early, and how you adjust so you can continue.
Intensity control is central to the method, and most training errors do involve running too fast. But even with correct intensity, the session can be wrong for the week you're in. After too little sleep, after a new strength block, after a shift from treadmill to hard asphalt, or after a couple of days with minor aches that change your stride without you noticing.
Two things make this difficult. The body changes all the time, often silently, and many of these changes don't force an obvious stop. They show up as a gradual shift in how the same sessions feel: slightly heavier breathing, slightly higher heart rate, a small drift in resting heart rate or HRV. If you respond by pushing through, you get less control, not more.
Part III covers total load management, muscular tolerance, and recovery in Practical terms. Not as health advice alongside the training, but as an integrated part of the method. If you want to train within the method regularly, you must manage transitions, tolerance, and adjustments just as systematically as you manage pace and rests.

As an elite runner, everything came back to one question: what is the highest intensity I can repeat, week after week, without paying for it later? That's the real sport—the one that sits underneath the races. Load, recovery, and health are in constant negotiation, and the conservative approach is often the only one that lets total load rise over months instead of collapsing after a few good weeks.
The goal is simple: stay training-ready. Transitions, muscle tone, the Golden Zone. Everything points toward the same outcome, the simplest one that matters most.
Can you keep going?
Back then I understood the physiology. I had tested the principles on myself, on training partners, on runners in Kenya. What I did not yet have was a clinical map of real life: jobs, families, uneven sleep, stress, travel, unpredictable weeks, and the quiet compromises that show up in the body long before an injury forces you to stop.
Thirteen years as a general practitioner gave me that map, no new principles, but the same principles seen from every angle, across ages and levels, with one extra thing that matters: a clear picture of where continuity breaks.
The patterns are almost boring in how reliably they repeat. A recreational runner trains steadily for two years, then jumps from four to six sessions per week while also increasing intensity, and Achilles pain shows up within weeks.
A veteran adds strength training in January but leaves the running untouched.
Spring arrives, and the treadmill becomes asphalt, the shoes change, pace creeps up, and the body gets no time to recalibrate.

The common denominator is simple: something changed, and the body did not get time to adapt. Sometimes the load itself is not even the main problem. Something else made the runner vulnerable first, and the training was simply the match. Blood work that could have revealed a deficit months earlier. Small changes in the stride pattern from minor aches that never felt serious enough to mention. A subtle drift in recovery that nobody treated as a signal. The runner thinks they're "fine" until the first workout that requires a clean landing and a calm tendon.
Over those years I learned which combinations are high-risk, which early signs get ignored, and how little it can take to tip the balance once the body is already stretched. I am not interested in overcomplicating this. I am interested in rules you can actually follow, the kind that protect training over time.
So I start this section where it matters most: with practical advice from the intersection of running and medicine-advice that strengthens the core of the method: durability and progression over time.
FOUR AREAS KEEP YOU RUNNABLE:
1.    Load and adaptation: Respect transitions.
2.    Injury prevention: Stop small issues from becoming layoffs.
3.    Return to training: Come back without restarting the cycle.
4.   Health checks: Track the few markers that actually matter.
1. Load and Adaptation
The most valuable part of general practice is not the single visit, but the timeline.
You see what people add, what they remove, what they change because life changes, and what the body does in response. If there is one lesson that keeps proving itself, it's this: injuries rarely happen at peak load. They happen in the transitions.
"Transitions" is not a vague concept. It's concrete. The shift from treadmill to outdoor running. New shoes. A new interval format you have not done before. A sudden move to faster running. Strength or plyometrics introduced without a ramp. Even a surface change can be enough to alter stress in a way the body notices, even if you don't.
But is the body not designed to adapt? Yes, and that's exactly the point. Adaptation is real, but it is not instant.

The muscular system, tendons, joints, and the nervous system adapt gradually.
Something as simple as muscle tone and muscle elasticity is adaptable and partly initiated by genetic processes. When the change is too abrupt, the body does not get the runway it needs for the gradual adaptation that makes the new load safe.
I remember the first spring sessions on a synthetic track after a winter of treadmill and road. Even with experience, I had to treat those first sessions with respect. The legs felt different. The impact loading was new. That experience stayed with me, and it's one of the reasons I take transitions seriously to this day.
Managing Transitions
After all these years, I am still careful that changes should be cautious and gradual. When I change shoes, increase load, or plan to run faster, I test first.
I pay attention to how the body reacts before I implement the change fully.
A principle I have followed consistently: maintain continuity in all training elements you want to keep. I still run fast intervals, progressive 45/15, every week, all year, never just periodically. This may sound risky, running near old race pace even now as a 47-year-old. But precisely because the body never loses the habituation, I avoid the dangerous new adaptation that so often leads to injuries. The body stays accustomed to a given load, year after year. I like the feeling of still being able to run fast. It reminds me of what was, and it feels good. I never allow myself to let it go.
Another strategy: introduce new elements with small doses. Walk the first day indoors with new shoes, then a few days later jog only the warm-up with them. Adapt to speed training by consistently adding one fast stride over one to two weeks before full sessions begin.
When something is nagging, the response is equally simple. Stop the session immediately. No heroics, no "just going to finish this one." Take one to two days off and start carefully again. This seemingly excessive caution, combined with systematic threshold training, has been decisive for being able to continue running injury-free, decade after decade.
What the Research Shows
In 2025, Frandsen and colleagues at Aarhus University published results from one of the largest running injury studies ever conducred. Over 5,200 runners from 87 countries were followed over 18 months in the study "How much running is too much? Identifying high-risk running sessions in a 5,200-person cohort study." What they found challenged much of the conventional understanding of how overload injuries develop.
The famous "10% rule" says you should never increase training by more than 10% per week. Sounds sensible-until you see the data. In this study, injury risk was largely linked to single sessions with too abrupt an increase in length, not just gradual changes in weekly volume. The numbers are stark:
*   Run 10-30% longer than your longest run in the last 30 days: injury risk was 64 % higher
*   Run 30-100% longer: risk was 52% higher
*   Double the distance: risk was 128% higher

2. Injury Prevention and Management
Beyond gradual buildup, it is sensible threshold-based training and good structure that matter most for staying injury-free. The effect of other measures (strength training, cold baths, massage, stretching) is moderate and highly individual compared to progression and continuity around threshold-based training. If you have to choose where to spend your energy, start there.
If you add something beyond that, emphasize shoes. The right choice of footwear has in recent years revolutionized the possibility of avoiding inju ries. When an injury does occur, first do a careful analysis. Look at patterns in the training. Be critical about when this actually started. Think back to similar problems.
Then a principle that perhaps many physician colleagues disagree with: is it possible to run through an injury with minimal total training load?

If you have a nagging knee or a sore Achilles, my experience is that small doses of running can be an important part of the rehabilitation itself. It must be so little that it does not worsen the injury, yet enough to maintain the running movement. For an Achilles injury, this might mean small runs of two to three minutes a few times a week before an alternative session with cycling and possibly eccentric training or physiotherapy.
This load should be under the best possible conditions: treadmill rather than outdoors, slight incline rather than flat, stable shoes, warm room. All of this contributes to being able to use running as part of rehabilitation.
My further experience is that this approach is also preventive for secondary injuries, which have an unfortunate tendency to appear when the original injury is finally healed. How often does it happen that as soon as training gets going after a knee injury, the hip starts to hurt? The strategy above helps you avoid that.
For those who are especially injury-prone, who struggle with repeated injuries, especially after longer periods of training, here is an injury prevention staircase. Each step strengthens the chance of staying healthy.
INJURY PREVENTION STAIRCASE
1.    Shoes. Invest in modern shoes with foam and a carbon plate. If you have been injured with one brand, switch to another.
2.    Flat training model over time. A flat structure where each week is relatively similar to the next can build a robust body and let load adaptation happen gradually: two to three threshold sessions per week, with minimal transitions and variation, where only easy sessions fill the gaps, for as long as four to eight months. The major advantage is muscular normalization. Many enter a training cycle with a muscular system where the glass is already almost full, often from too intensive training over time. A slightly too abrupt transition and the injury appears. With a longer cycle of identical structure around the threshold, the muscular system gets time to normalize and becomes far more robust if you later add variation and intensity.
3.    Lower the intensity. Be careful with correct intensity. Over a longer period, consider purchasing or renting a lactate meter. Then you know with certainty how accurately you are hitting the target.
4.    Treadmill. After injuries or operations, many find that treadmill running is less demanding than outdoor running. One to two interval sessions per week can ideally be on a treadmill. The foot strike feels gentler for many, and it is easier to control intensity.
5.    Systematic super-easy week every third to fourth week. Reduce everything: intensity, volume, and frequency. Combine with gradual transitions into and out of this week, and it can help prevent injuries over time.
6.    Stop immediately if you suspect injury. Transitions are not just about the sessions in isolation. Shoe changes, surface changes, treadmill to track. All transitions must be careful and gradual. Should you feel a nagging in a calf or hamstring, stop the session and take one to two training-free days.

If that's you, adjust the load with more shorter intervals and shorter rests, more elements of progression around the threshold, combined with regular X-sessions weekly.

4. Health Checks for Runners
Comprehensive studies show that general health checks without symptoms have no preventive benefit for the general population. But for those who train seriously, there are important exceptions. If you are going to maintain good training and the health benefits it provides, you should track iron levels-and preferably B12 and vitamin D as well.
Ferritin and Iron Deficiency
A study of 1,190 athletes showed that nearly 20% had iron deficiency, and these athletes had significantly lower VO, max values and a lower probability of reaching a VO_max above 50 ml/kg/min (Keller et al., 2024). Iron deficiency, with or without anemia, typically causes increased fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance. Systematic reviews confirm that iron treatment can reduce these symptoms (Auerbach et al., 2025).
Why do runners lose more iron? Hemolysis during landing means red blood cells are destroyed when the foot hits the ground. Iron is also lost through sweat and through the gastrointestinal system. Female runners face an added challenge with menstrual losses. Every time your foot hits the asphalt, you are crushing red blood cells. Multiply by 10,000 steps on a long run, and the scope becomes clear.
Ferritin is a protein that stores iron, and the blood level reflects the body's total iron stores. Standard laboratory lower limits are often set at 10-20 pg/L (10-20 ng/mL) for women and 20-30 |g/L (20-30 ng/ml) for men. But these reference ranges are based on the general population-not on the needs of someone who runs regularly.
Several studies confirm this gap. Hinton and Sinclair (2007) followed non-anemic endurance athletes with low ferritin and found that iron supplementation improved work economy and performance around the threshold level, even without large changes in hemoglobin. Peeling and colleagues (2008,
2014) showed how endurance sport easily causes iron deficiency via hemolysis, inflammation, and elevated hepcidin-a hormone produced in the liver that acts as the body's iron gatekeeper, regulating uptake and release of iron—often long before classic anemia occurs. They recommend that athletes without anemia also be followed closely with ferritin and other markers.
Many sports federations, including the Australian Institute of Sport, recommend that ferritin should be above 30-40 ng/mL. (g/L), preferably around 50 ng/mL, for athletes who train hard. Some sources point out that levels above 50-60 ng/mL can provide an important safety margin, especially for women.
I agree. When I write that ferritin below -30 ng/mL is clearly problematic for runners, and that 30-50 ng/mL is often suboptimal under heavy training, I'm talking about functional capacity as an endurance athlete, not the lower laboratory cutoffs used to define deficiency in the general population.
Vitamin D

Vitamin D is central in the prevention of stress fractures and especially important for female runners. Very low vitamin D can affect muscle strength and muscle fatigue. I believe it can also affect muscle tone and muscle recovery more broadly, although good studies have not been done on this.
It is not worth the risk to run with a level that is too low. To reduce the risk of stress fractures, runners should aim for at least 75 mol/L (30 ng/mL) in serum 25(OH)D. The optimal range for endurance athletes is probably 75-100 mol/L (30-40 ng/mL), in my experience higher than many active people have. For context, the US Endocrine Society defines insufficiency as 21-29 ng/mL and deficiency as 20 ng/mL or below.
I see it in my clinic. Even after the best Norwegian summers, with measurements taken in August, some patients consistently have low levels. I see years of data on my screen, and the patterns are surprisingly consistent. These patients should take supplements year-round as a simple measure to ensure a well-functioning body.
B12
B12 deficiency is perhaps less common than iron and vitamin D deficiency, but can be devastating for performance. Symptoms include fatigue, weakness, and reduced performance capacity. With pronounced deficiency, anemia develops with reduced oxygen transport. Vegetarians and especially vegans have increased risk, but runners who train hard and eat a narrow diet can also be vulnerable.
The standard lower reference limit is around 148 pmol/L (200 pg/mL) in many laboratories. However, athletes can still have functional B12 deficiency in the borderline range: serum B12 may appear adequate while tissue availability is insufficient relative to demand. If serum B12 is below -250 pmol/L (340 Pg/mL), it is reasonable to add homocysteine and, when available, methyl-malonic acid (MMA) to clarify status. If either marker is elevated, B12 def-ciency is likely despite a "borderline" serum value, and daily supplementation is typically recommended.
Recommended Targets
Ferritin: Aim for 50-60 g/L during high-volume training. Check 1-2 times per year.
Vitamin D: Aim for 75-100 nmol/L (30-40 ng/mL) 25(OH)D. Check yearly, more often if you tend to run low.
B12: Aim for at least ~250 pmol/L (~340 pg/mL), and preferably -300 pmol/L (~410 pg/mL). Check if you experience fatigue, have dietary risk factors, or persistent low energy.
What Separates Those Who Last
Those who succeed over time respect transitions and avoid abrupt changes.
They maintain continuity and always have a plan for difficult periods. They listen to the body and stop the session when something is off. They take health checks seriously if they train a lot, and they understand that sensible training over time beats intensive training in short bursts.
It can take months often four to six—to train yourself back after three to four weeks of interruption. Is that worth it, when a few extra rest days strategically placed might have prevented it? Or a slightly different balance of strength training and running?

In January 2001, I went to Kenya with a bag of standard mobility tests and a question that had been nagging me for months. I ran every elite runner I could find through the protocols. These were athletes known for fluid, efficient move-ment— the kind of form coaches hold up as ideal. Many had raced at the top level for years with barely an injury to speak of.
The results surprised me. In almost every direction, they were remarkably stiff. Hip flexors, hamstrings, ankles—numbers that would have alarmed any sports physiotherapist back home. Yet where it actually mattered, in the running movement itself, they were elastic, stable, and devastatingly efficient.
The question had been building for a while. When I was still competing, recovery meant stretching and strength work. As my times dropped and ambitions grew, the Norwegian Olympic Training Center took an interest and made mobility a priority—for running economy, they said, and injury prevention.
I spent half a winter following their protocols to the letter. Stretching sessions before and after runs. Mobility drills on rest days. The full regimen. Then doubt crept in: if mobility mattered this much, why did the runners with the best form and fewest injuseem to do so little of it? Kenya answered that.
I returned to Norway and quietly cut back on stretching. Then I cut back
further.
Eventually I stopped almost entirely.
What replaced it was a different kind of attention—not to flexibility, but to the things that genuinely seemed to govern whether a runner stayed healthy and kept improving. Load management. Muscle tone. The accumulation of stress across days and weeks, and the body's capacity to absorb it.

In the years since, I have watched the same pattern play out countless times.
Runners become consumed by everything surrounding training rather than the training itself. They convince themselves that intelligent programming is not enough, that they need strength circuits, stretching routines, foam rolling protocols, recovery gadgets.
The list grows, and the focus scatters.
I understand the impulse. These rituals feel like diligence. They create the satisfying sense that you are leaving nothing to chance. I have fallen into that trap myself, more than once. The lesson took years to fully absorb.
The Norwegian Method is built around maximizing the right training load-threshold work in a narrow intensity band, repeated with precision and consistency. That only works if recovery and prevention are treated with equal seriousness, not as an afterthought, not as a collection of rituals, but as a deliberate system that protects the body's capacity to do the work that matters.
That is why this chapter belongs here.
We cover five main areas: strength training and its place in running, stretching and flexibility, thermal therapy, modern running shoes, and energy balance.
Let's start with the question I am asked most often.
Strength Training
"But all elite runners do strength training!" I hear this constantly, and it's true, many do. Research suggests it can help. Meta-analyses on runners show small to moderate improvements in running economy, typically 2-8% after six to twelve weeks of strength or plyometric training (Balsalobre-Fernández et al.,
2016; Berryman et al., 2018). More recent work (Llanos-Lagos et al., 2024) indicates the effect is greatest at high loads (80% of one-rep max or above) and particularly at higher running speeds.
The numbers sound promising, but in my experience, strength training comes with hidden costs that rarely get discussed.
Several times during my career, we introduced structured strength pro-grams. Squats, deadlifts, running-specific movements, the standard prescrip-tion. Each time, the same thing happened: muscle tone increased, and hard running days had to be spaced further apart. The legs that had felt springy and responsive turned dense and slow to recover.
This is the trade-off nobody warns you about. Increased muscle tone, and the stress it places on tendon insertions and surrounding structures, is, in my view, one of the most underestimated risks when combining strength training with running.
The arithmetic is simple but unforgiving. When you're lifting heavy, you need more recovery between hard running sessions. More recovery means fewer quality threshold workouts. Fewer threshold workouts means reduced total volume in the zone that actually drives endurance adaptation. You gain something in the weight room and lose something on the road, and for most distance runners, what you lose matters more than what you gain.
I don't have all the answers, but I've seen this pattern often enough to urge caution.
A Practical Approach
If you want to try strength training, do it deliberately:
*   One to two sessions per week for six to twelve weeks during a building phase
*   High load (280% 1RM) or explosive plyometric work, the research supports this over lighter, higher-rep circuits

*   One session per week for maintenance once the block is complete
*   Pay attention to placement: for many runners, scheduling strength work directly after threshold sessions works better than on days between, preserving the principle of easy training on easy days
*   Emphasize eccentric work, particularly for hamstrings and calves, the muscle works while lengthening, which transfers well to the demands of running and may reduce injury risk
*   If you commit to strength training, do it year-round. Abrupt starts mid-season dramatically increase injury risk
*   Consider tapering or pausing during peak competition periods, but otherwise keep it as a fixed element in the annual plan
What I Learned the Hard Way
From 2001 to 2006, I made serious attempts at integrating strength and speed work into my training. It proved harder than I expected, especially once I understood the underlying logic. The entire training philosophy centers on the muscles as the limiting factor, and specifically on muscle tone. Nothing drives tone higher than heavy lifting.

Model A: After a threshold day.
Morning threshold session, then threshold plus strength or speed work in the evening. The advantage was concentration of load, you hammer the system once and recover. The disadvantage: muscle tone often stayed elevated into the next day, compromising what should have been easy running.
Model B: Before a threshold day.
Strength or speed work the evening before a threshold morning. The theory was that threshold work would help bring tone back down. Sometimes it did.
More often, it compromised the quality of the threshold session itself, the legs never quite found their rhythm.
Model C: After the X-session.
Hard X-session on Saturday, then strength or speed work immediately after or in the evening. Sunday easy. This concentrated the demanding work without bleeding into threshold days.
Model C worked best for me, but I didn't stick with it year-round, and looking back, I regret that. Abrupt starts pile new stress onto a system already carrying heavy load, and the body notices.

The Minimum Effective Dose
If you want to incorporate strength or speed training, commit to it consistently across the year. Abrupt transitions are where injuries happen. Individual differences in muscle fiber composition almost certainly affect who tolerates this kind of work well (explosive types often handle it better than pure endurance athletes) but the principle holds regardless.
My recommendation: chase the minimum effective dose at the lowest possible cost.
In practice, this means doing your strength and speed work at perhaps 80% of what you'd ideally like. You'll pay a fraction of the price compared to pushing all the way to one hundred. It's about respecting what the muscles can absorb alongside everything else you're asking of them. The weight room is not where distance runners win races, but a supplement, and supplements should support the main work, not compete with it.
When Strength Training Makes Sense
Age-related changes
Starting around age 30, muscle mass begins a slow decline, sarcopenia, the physiologists call it. The process accelerates after 50. Without intervention, you can lose 3-5% of muscle mass per decade. Elasticity fades too, in both muscles and tendons, raising injury risk and blunting your ability to generate force quickly.
For veteran runners, especially those over 50, strength training becomes a tool for preservation rather than performance. Were not necessarily talking about heavy sessions. Systematic maintenance work, performed consistently across the year, can slow the decline and keep the body robust enough to handle real training.
Documented weaknesses and asymmetries
Some runners carry clear deficits in specific muscle groups: hip abductors, hamstrings, glutes. Targeted strength work may be necessary to restore balance.
The same applies to runners with repetitive, asymmetric injuries that keep returning despite sensible training.
But before reaching for the barbell, i's worth asking: is this genuine muscle weakness, or is it the product of an unbalanced training structure? Many asymmetric injuries stem from volume or intensity that ramped up too fast, or from transitions that were too abrupt. In those cases, strength work will only mask the real problem, and may make things worse by driving up muscle tone.
Low bone density and stress fractures
Runners diagnosed with osteopenia or osteoporosis, or those with a history of stress fractures, may benefit from heavier strength work. Mechanical loading stimulates bone formation, but the total training load still needs careful scrutiny.
Many stress fractures happen precisely because the overall load climbed too high, not because the runner needed more time in the gym.
The Bottom Line - Strength training
Probably not necessary if you:
*   Are under 40
*   Are injury-free
*   Have room to add more running
Worth considering if you:
*   Are over 50 and noticing the effects of age
*   Have a history of injuries despite sensible training
*   Feel you've reached a genuine performance plateau
Yes, definitely if you have:
*   Known low bone density
*   Recurring asymmetric injuries that don't respond to load management
Stretching
"I need to get better at stretching." I hear this constantly from runners, especially those battling injuries. I understand the impulse. It feels intuitively right that mobile, supple muscles should make us better and more durable. Stretching delivers an immediate sense of well-being, the satisfying feeling of having done something positive for the body. No wonder it's become a fixed ritual for so many.
But when we look at what the research actually shows, the picture grows murkier.

What Does the Research Say?
A systematic review with meta-analysis published in Sports Medicine Open in 2025 examined the effect of stretching on running economy, how much oxygen you use at a given pace, the most objective measure of efficiency we have. The analysis pooled fifteen acute studies (stretching right before running) and two long-term studies (stretching programs over time), totaling 181 participants (Warneke et al., 2025).
The verdict was clear: static stretching, where you hold a position for 15-60 seconds, had no acute effect on running economy. Evidence for long-term benefit was thin. Whether you stretch before a run or follow a systematic program for months, it probably won't sharpen your efficiency.
The same holds for injury prevention. Large reviews show that static stretch-ing, before or after training, has no clear or practically meaningful effect on injury risk in runners. For many, this may be the most surprising finding, since injury prevention is usually the main argument in stretching's favor.
Static Versus Dynamic
It's worth distinguishing between different forms:
Static stretching, holding a muscle at length before or after running, delivers no meaningful improvement in running economy and has limited or no effect on injury prevention. Some studies have found that extensive static stretching right before high-intensity running can temporarily blunt force production, directly counterproductive.
Dynamic warm-up, controlled movements through a range of motion, can be used before fast sessions if you prefer. The benefit has more to do with neuromuscular activation and raising tissue temperature than with lengthening muscle. Even here, the measurable payoff for performance is modest. I's really about preparing body and mind for the work ahead. Before speed sessions or heavier strength work, it can be worthwhile, both as a warm-up and as a chance to scan for any warning signs before loading up.
Tendon Stiffness
Here's where things get interesting. Several studies have shown that higher tendon stiffness, especially in the Achilles, correlates with better running economy.
This may sound backwards if you've always believed loose and supple is the goal. The explanation is biomechanical, Tendons act like springs in the running stride. When the foot strikes the ground, kinetic energy is stored as the tendons stretch, much like compressing a coil. That energy is released in the push-oft.
An overly compliant muscle-tendon unit can actually be less efficient, because more energy bleeds away with each Landing.
This is why chasing ever-greater general flexibility isn't necessarily a worthy goal for runners. A degree of stiffness in the muscle-tendon system is functional, it enables more efficient force transfer and energy storage stride after stride.
It's also, I suspect, part of what I observed in Kenya all those years ago. Those runners weren't flexible by any conventional measure, but their stiffness was the right kind of stiffness, elastic where it mattered, stable where it counted.
Why Does the Myth Persist?
A few reasons:
First, stretching feels good. It creates a subjective sense of having done something positive for the body. That feeling is real, even if the performance benefit isn't.
Second, it's easy to explain injuries in hindsight by pointing to insufficient stretching. When a runner breaks down, "you didn't stretch enough" is simple and satisfying. The truth is almost always messier: volume that spiked too fast, poor training balance, inadequate recovery, or plain bad luck.
Third, stretching demands little knowledge or equipment. Easy to do, easy to prescribe. I's harder to say "examine your training structure and build load progressively with more threshold work," even though that advice would be far more useful.
Key point: Running is about specific adaptation. Thousands upon thousands of strides over time forge the efficiency you need. No amount of general stretching can substitute for that process. The body learns to run by running, not by sitting on a mat pulling at its hamstrings.
Unlike stretching, thermal therapy has stronger support in the literature and clearer practical value when applied correctly.

Thermal Therapy
1 used thermal therapy systematically throughout my career, and it remains a staple for many of today's best runners. The logic is straightforward, and the evidence backs it up.
When the body is immersed in cold water below 10-15°C (50-59°F), blood vessels in the skin and periphery constrict sharply. This curbs blood flow to stressed tissue, helping limit swelling and local inflammation. The low temperature also slows nerve signaling, which dials down pain perception.
Meta-analyses show small but real improvements in muscle soreness and perceived recovery after cold-water immersion, particularly in the 24 48 hours following a hard session (Moore et al., 2022; Choo et al., 2022). Best results come at 5-12°C (41-54°F) for 10-15 minutes.
The effect isn't dramatic, but it's consistent, and consistency matters when
you're trying to absorb high training loads week after week.
COLD WATER PROTOCOL
Some research suggests that trequent cold exposure may blunt strength adap-rations, but that's a minor concern for dedicated endurance runners. The more relevant consideration is timing. Use cold baths immediately after hard sessions, never between double threshold workouts, always after the last hard effort of the day. The goal is to accelerate the shift from stress to recovery, not to interrupt adaptation while it's still happening.
Systematic use of cold baths makes it far easier to modulate muscle tone across a training week. It's one of the few passive tools available besides massage, and unlike massage, it requires no appointment, no expense, and no special skill, just discipline and a bathtub full of cold water.
Hot Water Baths
Cold baths receive most of the attention, but hot baths have their place too.
A 2025 study by Dablainville and colleagues in the Journal of Physiology reported that muscle regeneration improved with hot-water immersion but was unchanged by cold water following simulated muscle damage.
The mechanisms differ, heat increases blood How and may accelerate the delivery of nutrients to damaged tissue, but the practical takeaway is similar: both hot and cold baths directly influence the muscles, and the muscles sit at the heart of both recovery and performance.
The timing differs from cold baths. Hot baths work best on easy training days and especially during demanding training blocks, when you want to bring muscle tone down as quickly as possible. This tracks with what many sprinters have found, and few athletes shoulder greater muscular load than sprinters.
I came to think of thermal therapy as a dial I could turn. Cold after hard days to limit inflammation and soreness. Hot on easy days to release tension and restore elasticity. Neither is magic, but used consistently and with purpose, both become genuine tools, not rituals.

Modern Running Shoes
Shoes may seem like equipment rather than recovery. In modern running, the line has blurred.
I's no exaggeration to say that the advances since 2018-19 represent the single greatest technological leap in the sport's history. When we talk about modern shoes with carbon plates and responsive foam delivering roughly 2-4% lower metabolic cost (Hoogkamer et al., 2018), we're talking about one of the most robust findings in recent running research.
Metabolic cost is energy expenditure per unit of distance, the oxygen and fuel you burn to cover a kilometer. A 2-4% reduction is substantial. For a 2:10 marathon, it could mean three to five minutes. For a 3:30 marathoner, perhaps six to eight.
These are not marginal gains, they are transformative.
But the effect is neither linear nor universal. It scales with running speed, gains are largest above about 16 km/h (10 mph). It varies with individual technique and foot strike. And perhaps most intriguing: it shifts with adaptation over time.
Early studies captured acute effects. We still know relatively little about how the body adjusts over months and years of consistent use. Among today's elite, more runners are growing conscious of this, rotating shoes to balance loading and unloading, reserving the fastest models for specific sessions.
I think that's wise. Deliberately alternating footwear based on load, session type, and training phase makes sense both for performance and for long-term tissue health.
Load, Biomechanics, and Injury Risk
When it comes to injury prevention, the picture grows more complex. Run-ning-economy research is clean, we can measure oxygen uptake with precision.
Injury-risk research is messier. Injuries spring from multiple causes, and rarely does a single variable tip the scales. What we know for certain: shoe type alone is a weak predictor of injury. Training load, total volume and how quickly it changes, matters far more.
But shoes aren't irrelevant. Studies show that carbon plates can dampen ground-reaction forces, and that a curved carbon plate trims peak forefoot pressure compared to a flat plate or none at all (Song et al., 2024). Lower peak forefoot pressure translates to less stress on the metatarsal heads, which should, in theory, cut stress-fracture risk in that region.
Beyond carbon: traditional EVA foam returns roughly 55-65% of the energy put into it. The rest dissipates as heat and permanent deformation.
PEBA-based foams can return 75-85%, sometimes more. The difference is palpable. The shoe gives back what you put in, rather than swallowing it.
My own experience lines up with the research. I used to need a long runway transitioning from treadmill to outdoor running each spring, often sensing minor injuries brewing as the surfaces changed. That problem has nearly vanished with newer shoes, even as I've gotten older. I see the same trend in clinical practice. Since modern running shoes arrived, Achilles injuries in particular have dropped off sharply among the recreational runners I treat.
Correlation isn't causation, but the timing is hard to ignore.
These days, the first piece of injury advice I offer, alongside training guid-ance, is an immediate switch to the best, newest models with carbon plates and modern foam. It's advice I never would have given before 2018.
Strategic Use
Carbon shoes aren't for every session. Deploy them strategically. At threshold pace and above, you get the greatest return from their help with speed and energy cost. The reduced muscular strain is a bonus when you're already pushing hard. This is where the shoes earn their price.
On easy long runs and recovery efforts, the picture is more nuanced. At low speeds, the raw pace benefit shrinks. The lighter toll on muscles and tendons can still pay off if you log heavy mileage or are injury-prone. Know your own body. If you've wrestled with metatarsal trouble or chronic issues from the knee down, wearing carbon shoes on some long easy outings may make sense.
If you're robust and injury-free, letting the foot muscles do honest work on easy days has value too.
Rotation and Phasing In
Rotate between two or three pairs with different profiles. This extends shoe life and introduces subtle variation in loading that can benefit tissues in the foot and lower leg. One pair slightly lower and more responsive, one more cushioned, one carbon pair for quality sessions. Phase in gradually. Don't swap shoes if your current ones are working and you're injury-free. This matters most when moving from traditional trainers to modern carbon shoes, or the reverse.
Start with 20-30% of weekly volume in the new shoes.
Add no more than 10-15% per week. If you pick up fresh warning signals from your foot, lower leg, or Achilles, hold off on increasing until the signals fade.

Shoe choice isn't the most consequential decision you'll make as a runner, volume and intensity distribution carry more weight. But shoes are a variable you control entirely, and the evidence supports the idea that smart choices yield measurable returns. Still, keep perspective. No shoe does the work for you. No shoe replaces consistent training over time. No shoe rescues poor planning. The shoes go on your feet. The work still has to go through your legs.
Recovery isn't only what you do after training, though. It's also what you
put back in.
Energy Balance
Energy balance may not be the most exciting topic in this chapter, but it touches everything else, and when it goes wrong, nothing else works quite right.
I've watched runners execute flawless threshold training, use cold baths religiously, own the best shoes on the market, and still grind themselves down because they simply weren't eating enough. The body can absorb remarkable amounts of training stress, but it cannot create energy from nothing. Fuel has to come from somewhere.
You don't need to obsess over calories or chase an ideal weight. But you should understand how much energy your body actually burns and needs, especially when the training load is high.

A 2024 study in Frontiers in Public Health by Tektunali Akman et al. found that a significant share of endurance athletes operate in "low energy availability," they don't take in enough to fuel both training and basic physiology.
Chronic under-fueling doesn't just slow recovery between sessions. It weakens immunity, saps motivation to train, disrupts hormone production, and leaves you generally flat and worn. The damage accumulates quietly, often invisible until something breaks.
The Weight Question
"Shouldn't I be as light as possible to perform my best?" I field this question constantly. The answer: it depends, and not in the way most runners expect.
Optimal race weight and optimal training weight aren't necessarily the same. I practiced this myself throughout my career. My winter weight ran several kilos above summer, by design. That buffer bought me better immune function through hard training blocks, more energy for quality sessions, and healthier hormone production.
Think of it as deliberate seasonal fluctuation. In fall and winter, while you're laying aerobic foundation and piling on volume, you can afford to carry a bit extra. The body has reserves to draw on. Recovery comes faster. Illness stays away. As race season nears, you can gently trim intake to reach competition weight if you choose. Hormonally, it often goes more smoothly when training Load dips and the body is in better balance. You're not fighting against physi-ology, you're working with it.
What matters most is finding an approach you can sustain. Extreme tactics rarely translate into better performance over the long haul. The runners who stay healthy and keep improving year atter year are rarely the ones chasing the lowest possible number on the scale. They're the ones who fuel the work.
Dynamic Rest Days
In a busy life, fixed rest days often make sense. Some days slot in more easily than others, and predictability has value. That said, I believe in dynamic rest days.
The idea is simple: instead of locking in which days you rest, you take time off when your body signals it needs a break. A subtle uptick in muscle tension during a session. An old niggle flaring without obvious cause. Step off immediately and take a day or two. If resting heart rate, HRV, or warm-up heart rate are off, that may be your cue. If a session feels inexplicably heavy-more than the training load would suggest-consider recovery rather than pushing through.
This requires attention, and it requires honesty with yourself. But it regulates training far more effectively than a rigid weekly schedule ever could.
Key point: The body doesn't know what day of the week it is. It only knows load and recovery. Listen to that conversation, and you'll make better decisions than any fixed plan can provide.
An Integrated Approach
Recovery and prevention are not about finding magic bullets. They are about building sustainable systems that support the training actually driving you forward.

Thermal therapy has documented benefits-use it with intention. Adequate energy intake is non-negotiable; the body cannot adapt to training it cannot fuel. Modern shoes can boost both performance and recovery; deploy them strategically. Strength training has a role for some, but weigh the cost against the reward, and remember that the cost is rarely as visible as the teward. Stretching? Do it if you enjoy it. Do not expect it to prevent injuries or make you faster.
With smart training and thoughtful recovery, day-to-day form will still swing within normal bounds. Some days feel effortless, others heavy. But the body responds and adapts. You absorb the work and come back ready for more.
That is the goal: a system that lets you train hard, recover well, and show up again tomorrow.
The trouble starts when normal variation drifts into decline. I have tracked runners who do most things right—train sensibly, use cold baths, eat enough, own good shoes, skip pointless stretching— yet slide, slowly but unmistakably, into a place where nothing clicks. Even easy jogs feel labored. Sessions that should be routine turn into battles. The body stops responding to the usual recovery measures. This is not ordinary fluctuation, but the body gradually losing its capacity to absorb load: the slide toward overtraining.
Paradoxically, the most dedicated and disciplined runners are often the ones who tip over the edge. They push when they should rest. They trust the plan when they should trust their legs.
The line between optimal load and overload is finer than most imagine.
